evidence_quotes.quote: Using data from an 18-month randomized trial, we estimate large and sustained impacts on water purification and child health of a program providing monthly coupons for free water treatment solution (diluted chlorine) to households with young children.
The program is more effective and much more cost-effective than asking Community Health Workers (CHWs) to distribute free chlorine to households during routine monthly visits.

That is because only 40% of households make use of free chlorine, targeting through CHWs is worse than self-targeting through coupon redemption, and water treatment promotion by CHWs does not increase chlorine use among free chlorine beneficiaries.

raw_response.plain_vs_narrow_note: Under the literal/plain wording of Criterion 2, comparing institutional distribution and targeting by Community Health Workers against administrative coupon redemption for free water treatment solution could plausibly be construed as an administrative or institutional delivery factor (yielding 'unsure' given the clean-water access framing). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, however, distributing a point-of-use health consumable (diluted chlorine) via clinic/program coupons versus CHW home visits and behavioural water-treatment promotion is health/WASH program delivery rather than a legal, regulatory, tenure, utility tariff/subsidy, enforcement/disconnection, or formal administrative rule governing water or sanitation service access, warranting exclusion (E03).
raw_response.rationale: This 18-month randomized controlled trial in Malawi evaluates a public-health program providing monthly coupons for free point-of-use water treatment solution (diluted chlorine) versus routine household distribution and promotion by Community Health Workers (CHWs). Even if household water purification is treated as borderline on water service access (C1 unclear, C4 yes), the study clearly fails the narrow rule-type Criterion 2 reading (E03 wrong exposure): it tests health-product delivery channels (coupons vs CHW visits) and behavioural promotion for bottled chlorine rather than any legal, regulatory, tenure/documentation, utility tariff/subsidy, disconnection, or formal administrative mechanism governing household or community water/sanitation service access.
